newsitem.title: USA: Enron to pay $440 million in gas supply settlement.
newsitem.headline: Enron to pay $440 million in gas supply settlement.

text.p: Enron Corp. said on Monday it will make a $440 million cash payment to Phillips Petroleum Co., Britain's BG Plc and Italian oil consortium Agip SpA to settle a lawsuit involving a gas supply contract.

Enron, one of the world's largest natural gas and electricity companies, said it will post an after-tax charge of $450 million, or $1.80 per share, for the settlement, resulting in a loss for the second quarter.
An Enron subsidiary had refused to buy British North Sea gas at a fixed price from the producers under the "take or pay" contract after gas prices had fallen substantially.

Under the settlement, the deal has been amended to a firm long-term supply contract and the fixed contract price reduced to reflect current market conditions for long-term gas sales, the companies said.
The total contract gas quantity from the offshore Judy and Joanne project, better known as the J-Block, will remain essentially the same, they said.
Phillips owns a 36.5 percent interest in J-Block and also operates it. Agip owns 33 percent, and BG Exploration & Production Ltd. 30.5 percent.
"Enron is pleased to remove this item of uncertainty for our company and our shareholders," said Kenneth Lay, chief executive of the Bartlesville, Okla.-based company.

"Renegotiation and settlement of the contractual issues now allow the gas to be taken at consistent volumes, assuring us a very significant, long-term supply at favourable fixed prices consistent with long-term contracts in the North Sea marketplace."
"The settlement concludes all J-Block litigation with Enron while achieving Phillips' objectives," the company said in a statement.
The settlement provides the J-Block owners with more flexibility to produce gas and liquids from fields in the surrounding area, the companies said.

Phillips said it will receive $160 million in the settlement. BG said separately its share will be $134.2 million. Both companies said they will recognise income associated with the payment over the remaining term of the supply contract.
Phillips said the decision of the High Court in London, expected June 3 in the lawsuit between Enron and the owners of the Central Area Transmission System, will not impact the settlement.
Enron said it expects to report a primary loss per share in the range of $1.40 to $1.45. The Houston-based company earned $222 million, or 88 cents per share, in the quarter ended March 31.
In July, and for the rest of 1997, J-Block gross production is expected to average 260 million cubic feet a day of gas and 95,000 barrels a day of liquids, Phillips said.
Initial gas sales will commence in June at lesser volumes, and liquids production will increase from the current 40,000 barrels-a-day level, it said.
Enron's stock fell 25 cents to $40.50, and Phillips rose 37.5 cents to $42.875 on the New York Stock Exchange in late morning trading.
